summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y2–Y3, US Grade 2): use addition to find the total of objects in a rectangular array (up to 5×5) and write an equation expressing the total as a sum of EQUAL addends, then bridge to the multiplication fact. The core insight is that each row of the array contributes one equal addend, so reading an array row by row turns it into repeated addition (4+4+4=12) and then into 3×4. Equality of the rows is what makes it a multiplication situation, so a ragged (unequal-row) arrangement serves as the key non-example.
misconceptions: Adding UNEQUAL groups and still writing it as a single multiplication (missing the equal-addends requirement).
Counting every object individually rather than adding equal rows.
Confusing the number of rows with the number in each row when writing the equation.
Not connecting the repeated-addition equation to the multiplication (seeing them as separate).
Miscounting by losing track of which rows have been added (no systematic row-by-row approach).

activities.title: Sum the rows: build the equal-addend equation from an array
steps: Look at a 3×4 array (3 rows, 4 dots in each row) and point to one row to establish that it holds 4 dots.
Add the array one row at a time, saying and writing the running total: 4, then 4+4, then 4+4+4 = 12 — one addend per row.
After writing 4+4+4=12, write the matching multiplication 3×4=12 and say which number tells how many rows and which tells how many are in each row.
Read the same array by columns instead and write it as 3+3+3+3 (four 3s), noticing you get 12 again.
Now try a ragged arrangement where one row has 4 and another has 5; attempt to write a single equal-addend equation and explain why it will not form.
activities.insight: Each equal row of an array is one equal addend, so adding the rows gives the total; the multiplication fact is just the shorthand for adding equal rows, and this only works when the rows are equal.

activities.title: Draw an array for a given equation
steps: Given the equation 5+5+5+5, draw a rectangular array that matches it (four rows of five, or equivalently five columns of four).
Say aloud which part of the equation is the number of rows and which is the amount in each row.
Write the multiplication fact for your array (4×5 or 5×4) and check the total matches 20.
Explain why your drawing shows equal rows and how that connects back to the repeated addition.
activities.insight: Children can move in both directions — from array to equation and from equation to array — which shows they understand the equal-groups structure rather than just reading one off the other.

activities.title: Match and complete: array ↔ equal-addend equation ↔ multiplication
steps: For a shown array, fill in the blanks of the equal-addend equation (__ + __ + __ = __).
Write the matching multiplication fact for the same array.

From a set of candidate equations, choose the one that matches a given equal-rows array; include a distractor that uses unequal addends (e.g., 3+4+5), which would correspond to a ragged arrangement and does not match.
Explain why the unequal-addend distractor cannot represent the equal-rows array as a single equal-addend equation.
activities.insight: Recognising and completing the correct equal-addend equation (and rejecting an unequal-addend distractor) confirms the array-to-repeated-addition bridge and the equal-addends requirement.

checkQuestion: Look at this array — 3 rows with 4 dots in each row. Sam counted the dots one by one and got 12. Priya wrote 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 without counting them all. Is Priya's way correct, and why does adding 4 three times work for this array?
checkAnswer: Yes — every row has the same number, 4, and there are 3 rows, so the total is 4 added three times. Equal rows let you add the row-amount repeatedly instead of counting every dot.
